name: N-Acetylcysteine

lead: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is a modified form of the amino acid cysteine. It is an established medicine used as the antidote for acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose and as a mucus-thinning agent, and is also sold as a supplement.

In recovery and appearance communities it is used as a glutathione precursor and antioxidant. Beyond its approved uses, evidence for skin, hair or recovery benefits is limited, though it has been studied for psychiatric and compulsive-behavior conditions.

paras: NAC supplies cysteine, the rate-limiting building block for glutathione synthesis, and can also act as a direct reducing agent and modulate glutamate signaling.

Common side effects are nausea and other gastrointestinal upset; a sulfur odor is commonly noted. Intravenous use carries anaphylactoid reaction risk. Its US regulatory status as a supplement has been disputed because it is also an approved drug, though it remains widely available.

lead: N-acetylcysteine (NAC, acetylcysteine) is the N-acetyl derivative of the amino acid L-cysteine. It is an established medicine, used as the antidote for paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose and as a mucolytic that loosens thick mucus in chronic lung disease, and it is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines. It is also widely sold as a dietary supplement [1].

In recovery, fitness and appearance communities NAC is used as a glutathione precursor and antioxidant, often as a liver-protection supplement during hormone or anabolic-steroid use, and sometimes for mood and compulsive behaviour. Its core medical uses are supported by clinical practice and trials. For other uses, including skin, hair and exercise recovery, evidence is limited: Wikipedia notes only preliminary research on androgenetic alopecia, and psychiatric uses are described as preliminary [1].

Common side effects are nausea and vomiting by mouth, and rash or a non-immune anaphylactoid reaction is possible with intravenous use [1]. Its status as a supplement in the United States has been contested because it is also an approved drug [1].
infobox: Prescription drug and dietary supplement; US supplement status disputed [1]
On WHO List of Essential Medicines [1]

paras: NAC is given intravenously or orally as the antidote for paracetamol overdose. The toxic metabolite NAPQI normally conjugates with glutathione, and in overdose glutathione stores run out; NAC replenishes glutathione and enhances non-toxic metabolism [1]. Inhaled NAC is used as a mucolytic, cleaving disulfide bonds in mucus proteins to reduce viscosity, in conditions such as COPD and bronchitis [1]. A 2024 review describes its efficacy in acetaminophen overdose, cystic fibrosis and COPD as well established, and lists many other conditions for which it may be an adjunct [2]. Wikipedia notes that a 2013 Cochrane review in cystic fibrosis found no evidence of benefit from inhaled NAC [1].

Other experimental or preliminary uses include non-acetaminophen acute liver failure, ototoxicity prevention, psychiatric conditions such as obsessive-compulsive disorder and trichotillomania, and as an adjunct in addiction, though evidence for gambling, methamphetamine and nicotine addiction was described by Wikipedia as not supportive [1].

NAC supplements are taken as antioxidants, as liver protection and for mood. Forum users list it among liver-support supplements during testosterone or oral anabolic use, and for glutamate-related effects in insomnia and mood [3][4][5][6]. Wikipedia reports preliminary research on NAC for androgenetic alopecia, with or without minoxidil, and on hearing protection [1]. No trial in the sources reviewed shows a cosmetic effect of oral NAC on skin or hair in healthy people.

NAC is a prodrug of L-cysteine, the rate-limiting precursor for the antioxidant glutathione, and its thiol group can directly reduce free radicals [1][7]. A 2021 review states that its antioxidant role stems mainly from raising intracellular glutathione, and that it can lower TNF-alpha, IL-6 and IL-1 beta by suppressing NF-kappa B [7]. Wikipedia also describes effects on glutamate signalling through the cystine-glutamate antiporter and modulation of dopamine release [1]. A 2021 pharmacology paper proposes that hydrogen sulfide and sulfane sulfur species contribute to its mechanism [8].

Oral bioavailability is low, about 6-10 percent, because of extensive first-pass metabolism, while intravenous dosing gives nearly complete bioavailability; after a single intravenous dose the half-life was reported as 5.6 hours [1].

Acetaminophen poisoning is the best-supported indication, and the treatment's effect on preventing liver injury is described in a 2022 comprehensive review [9]. Mucus hypersecretion in the airways has been examined in a 2024 systematic review [10].

In acute liver failure not caused by acetaminophen, a double-blind randomised trial reported improved transplant-free survival with intravenous NAC in early-stage cases [11], and a 2022 meta-analysis of five prospective studies (672 patients) found improved transplant-free survival but not overall survival [12]. In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a 2012 randomised trial tested a combination of prednisone, azathioprine and NAC against placebo [13]. A 2024 trial examined adjunctive NAC and lung function in pulmonary tuberculosis [14].

In polycystic ovary syndrome, a 2025 meta-analysis of 22 studies (2,515 participants) found that NAC was associated with higher progesterone and endometrial thickness, with no significant differences in estradiol, SHBG or FSH [15]. A systematic review of nutrition in bipolar disorder found variable and mainly non-significant effects of NAC and other supplements [16], and Wikipedia describes add-on NAC as reducing depression scores in meta-analyses with low-quality evidence but without improving response and remission [1]. Wikipedia states that studies in COVID-19 did not show improved outcomes by common measures [1]. A 2021 review adds that, despite relevant therapeutic potential in experimental studies, effectiveness in clinical trials across many conditions remains limited [7].

Human research is extensive. Randomised trials and meta-analyses cover non-acetaminophen acute liver failure [11][12], idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis [13], pulmonary tuberculosis [14], polycystic ovary syndrome [15][17], substance use disorders on methadone maintenance [18] and aluminium phosphide poisoning [19]. Registered trials include COVID-19 studies (NCT04792021, NCT04419025) [20][21], a smoking trial (NCT02124525) [22], studies in autism spectrum disorder (NCT05494398, NCT04278898) [23][24] and a trial of ototoxicity protection (NCT01271088) [25].
No studies were found of oral NAC supplementation for appearance outcomes in healthy people; the nearest research is preliminary work on androgenetic alopecia noted by Wikipedia [1].

Oral NAC commonly causes nausea, vomiting, rash and fever; intravenous formulations most often cause rash, urticaria and itching, and intravenous NAC can cause a rate-related anaphylactoid reaction, usually mild; inhaled forms can cause nausea, rhinorrhoea, drowsiness and bronchospasm [1]. It appears to be safe in pregnancy [1]. Nitroglycerin may interact, possibly causing low blood pressure and headache [1].

Wikipedia also describes animal findings: very high doses in mice, equivalent to about 20 grams a day in humans, were associated with pulmonary artery hypertension through a metabolite, with implications for long-term human use not investigated, and NAC taken four hours after alcohol worsened liver damage in mice [1]. A 2021 review calls the safety profile well established, with toxicity uncommon and dependent on route and high doses [7].

NAC was patented in 1960 as a mucolytic and came into medical use in 1968 [1]. Grokipedia attributes its development to Aaron Sheffner at Mead Johnson and says the US FDA approved it for inhalation in 1963 under the name Mucomyst; these details are from an AI-generated source and are unverified here [26].

In the late 1960s the popularity of acetaminophen led to rising overdose liver injury; a 1974 finding on the mechanism through cytochrome P450 led to treatment with glutathione-like reducing agents. A 1977 report described oral NAC preventing overdose hepatotoxicity in the US, while in the UK intravenous NAC (Parvolex) was found more effective with fewer side effects than alternatives. An intravenous product, Acetadote, was approved in the US in 2004 [1].

Early work from 1989 characterised its antioxidant reactions with hydrogen peroxide and hydroxyl radical [27], and 1990s studies used NAC as a tool to probe oxidative signalling in cells, including NF-kappa B activation [28].

Wikipedia reports that Amazon removed acetylcysteine products from sale in the US in 2021 after the FDA took the position that it is a drug rather than a supplement; in April 2022 the FDA released draft guidance on products labelled as supplements containing NAC, and Amazon re-listed NAC products in August 2022 [1].

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and fitness communities
paras: On T Nation, NAC appears as a liver-protection supplement during testosterone use, in recipes for mood or sleep, and in long supplement lists. One user says a clinical nutritionist prescribed 1,500 mg to protect the liver because of daily Tylenol use [4]; another says NAC 'should decrease' elevated ALT during a testosterone cycle [5]; another thread advises it for depression [6]. Posters also share research on NAC infusion attenuating early adaptive responses to exercise in human muscle [29] and note NAC in an anabolic steroid user's daily log.

lore.intro: On T Nation, NAC is mostly a background supplement: a liver-protection add-on during testosterone or anabolic use, and a mood or sleep adjunct. [4][5][6][3]
